question:
A recurring workflow in our team passes work from one person to the next, and today only two senior developers know how it goes. I want to write it down so that new developers and automated coding agents follow it the same way every time: what must the write-up state, and in what forms can it be written?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
[JEV filter] kept 12 of 12 guidelines (JEV 'lenient' score > 0.5)

# Guidelines
- Define the workflow as a 'process': state its required inputs, the transforming activities performed, and the outputs generated — because a process is precisely '[SWEBOK excerpt 2ff433908b429c69cdbc]', and its description must cover all three elements. (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Engineering Processes and System Lifecycles/Software Engineering Process Definition and Structure/Software Engineering Process Definition.md; root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Engineering Processes and System Lifecycles/Software Engineering Process Definition and Structure/Software Process Definition and Components.md) [JEV 0.96]
- Explicitly document the hand-off points: because '[SWEBOK excerpt 95c25f0e7764637e7e2a]', the write-up must specify what artifact or result leaves one person's hands and enters the next person's step. (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Engineering Processes and System Lifecycles/Software Engineering Process Definition and Structure/Software Process Definition and Components.md) [JEV 0.87]
- Include controls (directives and constraints) and enabling mechanisms ([SWEBOK excerpt ded2208f432cf43250ed]) alongside each activity, as these are recognised parts of a complete process description. (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Engineering Processes and System Lifecycles/Software Engineering Process Definition and Structure/Software Process Definition and Components.md) [JEV 0.93]
- Record the rationale for every non-trivial decision in the workflow. Prior assumptions, alternatives considered, and trade-offs analysed should be captured so that future developers (or agents) who modify the workflow understand why each step is the way it is. (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Recording Design Rationale for System Maintainability.md; root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Software Design Documentation and Communication Methods/Recording Software Designs.md) [JEV 0.97]
- Capture the vocabulary of the problem domain in the write-up. Work products should record '([SWEBOK excerpt 40320ec9774e6cffdc66]; ([SWEBOK excerpt 59eaedf69004d1128ce1].' (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Software Design Documentation and Communication Methods/Recording Software Designs.md) [JEV 0.98]
- Choose from several recognised notation forms for the write-up: natural language (textual lists of [SWEBOK excerpt f864e968f8f70dfb2aaa], IDEF0, Petri nets, UML activity diagrams, or Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN). (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Process Foundations and Measurement/Software Process Infrastructure Tools and Notations.md) [JEV 0.95]
- Support the textual or informal write-up with model-based artifacts where possible. Document-based artifacts that rely solely on natural language and informal diagrams risk introducing 'ambiguity and incompleteness'; model-based design reduces those risks and is better suited to automated tooling. (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Software Design Documentation and Communication Methods/Software Design Notations and Model-Based Approaches.md) [JEV 0.94]
- Use UML activity diagrams to show the flow of the workflow from activity to activity, including [SWEBOK excerpt 621bbd34c57820977bd6] — making the sequence unambiguous for both human readers and automated agents. (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Activity and Interaction Diagrams in UML.md) [JEV 0.91]
- If the workflow involves software components, supplement the process description with structural notations such as interface description languages (IDLs), structure charts, or entity-relationship diagrams to describe the interfaces and calling structures of any components involved. (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/System Design Documentation and Notation Tools/Data Modeling and Software Component Documentation.md) [JEV 0.91]
- Use both structural and behavioral notations in combination, since '[SWEBOK excerpt b39e8bb1b182c06a4843]' — structural ones to describe how the workflow is organised, and behavioral ones to represent what happens at each step. (source: root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Software Design Documentation and Communication Methods/Software Design Notations and Model-Based Approaches.md) [JEV 0.93]
- Consider adopting a formal process-definition tool (e.g., a BPMN toolkit) to support the definition and ongoing maintenance of the workflow documentation, as the BoK notes that software process infrastructure includes such tools specifically for this purpose. (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Process Foundations and Measurement/Software Process Infrastructure Tools and Notations.md) [JEV 0.93]
- Align the write-up with the life-cycle concept: since simply defining individual process activities '[SWEBOK excerpt 691d88c47b7d33009c03]', the documentation should also define the broader lifecycle context — including constraints — within which the workflow sits. (source: root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Software Engineering Processes, Lifecycles, and Measurement/Software Engineering Processes and System Lifecycles/Life Cycle Definition and Process Categories in Software Engineering.md) [JEV 0.95]
